title: Treating pasty vent in chicks
subtitle: Clearing a blocked vent in a new chick before it causes fatal obstruction.
excerpt: Pasty vent is a common problem in the first week of life where faeces dry over the chick's vent opening and block it. Left untreated, it is fatal: the chick cannot pass droppings and becomes lethargic within hours. The fix is simple: soften the blockage with warm water and remove it gently, without pulling at the tissue beneath.
sourceNotes: Gail Damerow, Storey's Guide to Raising Chickens (2017), chapter on chick care. University of Florida Extension, Backyard Poultry Production in Florida, chick brooding section (2022). Royal Veterinary College, Small Flock Poultry Health Advice (2023).

glossaryTerms.definition: A condition in newly hatched chicks where loose or sticky droppings dry over the vent opening, creating a hard paste that can block the passage entirely. Also called pasted vent or vent gleet in older birds.
The external opening of the cloaca in poultry, through which droppings, urine, and eggs pass. In a healthy chick it is clean, pink, and open.

content.text: is a blockage of dried droppings over the chick's vent opening. It is most common in the first three to five days of life, especially in chilled, stressed, or shipped chicks. The problem sounds minor but is quickly fatal: a chick with a fully blocked
cannot defecate, becomes toxic, and dies within 24 to 48 hours of the blockage forming.

Check every chick's vent at least once daily for the first week. Pick each one up, hold it gently with the head in your palm and the abdomen facing you, and look at the vent. It should be clean, pink, and open. A paste of dried dropping over the opening, even a small one, needs treating immediately.
Hold the chick in one hand, supported and calm. Have a small bowl of warm water and a clean soft cloth or cotton wool pad ready.

Soak the paste gently with warm water on the cloth. Hold the warm damp cloth against the blockage for 30 seconds. Do not pull at the paste dry: the chick's thin skin tears easily and you may remove tissue along with the paste.
Once the paste is soft, gently roll or wipe it free. Most paste should come away in one piece once well softened. If it does not come away cleanly, soak for another 30 seconds and try again.
Check that the vent is now open and that the chick passes a dropping within the next hour. A chick that was seriously blocked may produce a large messy dropping soon after the blockage clears.
Apply a thin layer of petroleum jelly (Vaseline) around the vent after clearing. This prevents paste from adhering so firmly the next time.
Return the chick to the brooder immediately and make sure it finds heat and water.

Chilled chicks, chicks stressed during shipping, and chicks on a cold damp floor are most susceptible. A brooder temperature that is too low or too uneven produces looser droppings that are more likely to smear and dry. Address the root cause alongside the treatment:
Check that the brooder is at the correct temperature at chick level (around 35 degrees in week one).
Ensure fresh clean water is always available and close to the heat source.
Change the bedding as soon as it becomes damp or fouled.

attrs.cue: Paste returns within hours of being cleared
attrs.cause: Chick still stressed or cold; droppings still loose
attrs.fix: Reapply petroleum jelly around the vent after each clearing. Isolate the chick under the warmest part of the brooder with easy access to water. If loose droppings persist beyond 48 hours, check for coccidiosis in older chicks.

attrs.cue: Skin is bleeding slightly after paste removal
attrs.cause: Paste was removed before sufficiently softened, or the skin is very fragile in a very young chick
attrs.fix: Clean the area gently and apply a very small amount of petroleum jelly. Keep a close eye on the wound: other chicks will peck at any visible injury. Isolate if necessary.
